advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm/document that the REBAR_LLM_MODEL fan-out intentionally drops REBAR_LLM_MODEL_PROVIDER/REBAR_LLM_BASE_URL, and add a caveat for legacy local-server operators (or fan those out too).
evidence: `model = raw.get("model") or fallback_default or _DEFAULT_MODEL_BY_CLASS[name]` — only `model` receives `fallback_default`; `provider`/`endpoint` (lines 157-158) are unaffected by the fan-out
`_deprecated_bare_model` returns just `raw.strip()` (model_classes.py:216), never the provider/base_url companions
docs/llm-framework.md previously documented the local-server recipe as `REBAR_LLM_MODEL=local-model REBAR_LLM_MODEL_PROVIDER=openai REBAR_LLM_BASE_URL=...`, i.e. the three were a set
ADR 0057 frames fan-out as 'an operator who set only the old knob has it honoured everywhere' but does not address the multi-knob local-server case
advisory.finding: The REBAR_LLM_MODEL fan-out into model_classes carries only the `model` field to the default position; it does not carry the legacy companion knobs REBAR_LLM_MODEL_PROVIDER / REBAR_LLM_BASE_URL. An operator who ran a local OpenAI-compatible server via the old trio (REBAR_LLM_MODEL=local-model + REBAR_LLM_MODEL_PROVIDER=openai + REBAR_LLM_BASE_URL=...) has only the bare model fanned out to the class slots; provider/endpoint stay None and are re-inferred, so the class-resolution path can silently target the wrong provider/endpoint for that operator.
scenarios: An operator on the deprecated local-server config (bare model + provider + base_url) upgrades; class-based resolution infers a provider from `local-model` (or none) instead of honoring the intended openai/endpoint.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Reword docs/llm-example-configs.md intro so the `[tool.rebar.llm]` vs `[tool.rebar.llm.model_classes]` table naming matches the examples.
evidence: Intro: 'Four complete, paste-able `[tool.rebar.llm]` configurations. Each is a **whole** table'
Examples 1-3 use `[tool.rebar.llm.model_classes]` and example 4 uses `[tool.rebar.llm.model_classes.frontier]` etc. — sub-tables of `[tool.rebar.llm]`, not the `[tool.rebar.llm]` table itself
advisory.finding: docs/llm-example-configs.md opens by describing all four examples as complete `[tool.rebar.llm]` tables, but examples 3 and 4 are actually `[tool.rebar.llm.model_classes]` / `[tool.rebar.llm.model_classes.<class>]` sub-tables, not `[tool.rebar.llm]` tables. The intro's 'whole table, not a fragment' framing is slightly inaccurate for those two.
scenarios: A reader copies an example expecting a full `[tool.rebar.llm]` block and is briefly confused by the header mismatch.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace test_the_registry_comment_no_longer_claims_permanent_only's comment-text grep with a behavioural assertion (e.g. REGISTRY[key].permanent is False plus the emitted message wording via warn_deprecated) instead of grepping _deprecations.py source prose.
evidence: assert "holds ONLY these permanent" not in src.replace("\n", " ").replace("  ", " ")
The grepped tokens are free-text in a comment block (_deprecations.py:76-95); no parser/validator/registry branches on them, so this is source-grepping, not a structural-boundary assertion.
advisory.finding: test_the_registry_comment_no_longer_claims_permanent_only asserts on the TEXT OF A CODE COMMENT in the source-under-test (_deprecations.py), not on any executable behaviour. It reads the source and asserts the phrase 'holds ONLY these permanent' is absent and that 'supersession|superseded' is present. No non-human consumer reads that comment; it is grepping source-code prose, so it is a change-detector that breaks on any behaviour-preserving reword of the comment and detects no regression in the deprecation behaviour.
scenarios: A maintainer rewords the registry comment (behaviour unchanged) and this test fails.
The _scheduled entry's behaviour regresses but the comment text is untouched — the test still passes, catching nothing.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Downgrade the .md prose greps (ADR alternatives/rename wording, per-doc 'deprecated' word, and the model_classes/class-name substring counts) to structural checks a machine actually consumes, or accept them as non-blocking coverage notes rather than wording-coupled assertions.
evidence: assert re.search(r"rejected|Alternatives", text, re.I) and assert re.search(r"rename", text, re.I) (ADR prose)
if bare.search(text) and not re.search(r"deprecated|DEPRECATED", text): stale.append(rel) (per-doc word grep)
assert text.count("model_classes") >= 4 and for cls in (...): assert text.count(cls) >= 4 (substring counts over prose)

Unlike test_the_env_read_is_a_string_literal (which I confirmed is read by scripts/gen_env_registry.py's static scanner at gen_env_registry.py:114-118 — a real non-human consumer), these grep prose no machine parses.
advisory.finding: Three doc-prose grep tests (test_the_adr_records_the_decision_and_the_rejected_alternatives, test_every_prose_doc_marks_the_variable_deprecated, test_the_four_example_configs_exist_and_are_complete_tables) assert on human-facing prose tokens in .md files ('rejected|Alternatives', 'rename', 'deprecated', section labels, bare class-name substring counts). No non-human consumer (parser/validator/CI that branches on the exact value) reads these tokens, so per the Rule-5 litmus they are change-detectors of the author's wording, not structural-boundary assertions — they break on a harmless reword and detect no behavioural regression.
scenarios: An author rewords the ADR ('Alternatives considered' -> 'Options weighed') or a guide's deprecation note, behaviour unchanged, and the test fails.
A doc could satisfy text.count(cls) >= 4 with incidental mentions rather than a usable config, so the count guard does not actually verify the four tables are complete/paste-able.
